title: Bengaluru's Startup Boom Has a Health Problem Nobody Talks About
excerpt: As Karnataka cements its position as India's startup capital with a $152.8 billion ecosystem, founders and techies are increasingly sounding the alarm about burnout, toxic work culture, and physical health deterioration.
body:
• Bengaluru ranks 15th globally in the Startup Ecosystem Index with a $152.8 billion ecosystem value, and Karnataka hosts 39% of India's GenAI startups.
  • Multiple founders and tech workers have gone viral describing health breakdowns tied to the city's always-on work culture — from burnout and chronic exhaustion to cardiovascular episodes.
  • A 24-year-old machine learning engineer at an AI startup died in Bengaluru in 2025 after struggling with overwhelming workloads, highlighting the human cost of hustle culture.
  • Founders are increasingly leaving the city for places like Goa and Pune, citing an inability to disconnect and a culture that equates identity with professional output.

Bengaluru is having it both ways — and paying for it. India's startup capital, which secured 89 deals worth $823 million in Q1 2026 alone and ranks second in Asia for AI innovation, is simultaneously producing a steady stream of viral confessionals from founders and tech workers whose health has cratered under the weight of its relentless work culture.

The Numbers Behind the Boom

Karnataka's dominance in India's startup ecosystem is not in question. The state hosts 39% of India's Generative AI startups, according to the Economic Survey 2025-26. Bengaluru ranks 15th globally in the Startup Ecosystem Index with a $152.8 billion ecosystem value, according to the Global Startup Ecosystem Report 2026 unveiled at VivaTech Paris. The city has over 16,000 startups and more than 550 Global Capability Centres.

In Q1 2026, Bengaluru accounted for 33% of total startup funding in the country, according to data reported by AInvest. Chief Minister Siddaramaiah attributed this to political stability, transparent governance, and a robust legal framework.

The Health Cost Nobody Budgets For

But underneath the funding rounds and valuation milestones, a different narrative keeps surfacing on LinkedIn, Reddit, and X. Tech workers and founders are documenting physical and mental health breakdowns they attribute directly to Bengaluru's work culture.

One founder described the city's pull as a kind of infection. Ankit Vengurlekar, who moved from Bengaluru to Goa, wrote on LinkedIn that whether on pickleball courts, during morning runs, at dinner, or even on dates, conversations in Bengaluru inevitably turn to work, salaries, and opportunities. He called it the "Bengaluru virus" — a toxic inability to switch off work talk regardless of setting.

"Yes, the coffee's still strong, the startups are still pivoting, and the LinkedIn posts continue to thrive! But under all that hustle lies a deep, collective burnout."

— Karan Raghani, Startup Founder, after 10 days in Bengaluru

After spending 10 days meeting founders, marketers, and techies, startup founder Karan Raghani posted that the city is "exhausted," with people "surviving on caffeine, wifi drops, and a distant dream of work-life balance."

When Burnout Turns Fatal

The consequences extend beyond discomfort. In 2025, Nikhil Somwanshi, a 24-year-old machine learning engineer at Ola's AI venture Krutrim, was found dead in Bengaluru. He had reportedly struggled with overwhelming workloads and relentless pressure, according to a detailed report by Rest of World. Krutrim's founder Bhavish Aggarwal had publicly derided work-life balance as "a Western cultural import" and advocated for a 70-hour workweek.

In another case reported by MedBound Times, a Bengaluru techie suffered a cardiovascular episode during a Google Meet after months of sustained verbal harassment from a CEO. He experienced chest tightness and shortness of breath before collapsing, requiring emergency medical attention.

The Exodus Has Begun

Some are voting with their feet. Dhruv Suyamprakasam, CEO of telemedicine startup iCliniq, left Bengaluru twice within 16 months, telling Livemint that the city's "grow fast, fail fast" pressure did not align with a healthcare business that demands trust and precision. An entrepreneur couple told NDTV they were leaving because pollution was "slowly killing" them — Bengaluru's AQI hit 297 in February, equivalent to smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

A Paradox With No Easy Fix

The tension is structural. The same density of ambition that makes Bengaluru the country's innovation engine also creates an environment where health becomes collateral damage. Karnataka's IT Minister Priyank Kharge has focused on deeptech investment and founder-friendly policies, but no public initiative has directly addressed the health crisis among the city's tech workforce. Until that changes, Bengaluru's startup story remains incomplete — brilliant on the balance sheet, brutal on the body.
nri_angle: Many NRIs considering reverse migration to Bengaluru's startup scene face the same health tradeoffs — the city's work culture mirrors Silicon Valley's intensity but with fewer institutional safeguards.
author: Diaspora Desk
